When you want to clarify which person or thing you are talking about, you use a relative clause.

You can begin a relative clause with who for people, which for things or that for either people or things.

You put the relative clause immediately after the noun it talks about.
A subject relative clause describes the subject of the clause.

Example:
The woman who/that lives next door to me brought me a cake.
The clause - who/that lives next door - refers to the woman. Who/that is the relative pronoun. It is also the subject of the clause. Who lives next door? The woman.
An object relative clause describes the object of the clause.

Example:
The apartment which/that we rented was near the center of the city.

The clause - which/that we rented - refers to the apartment. Which/that is the relative pronoun. We is the subject of the clause. Apartment is the object of the clause. What did we rent? The apartment.

Talking about Wishes and Imaginary Situations

You use wish when you are sorry that things are not different. You hoped for a different past or present.

You use the second conditional to talk about imaginary situations in the present of future.

Wish form:
Wish + that-clause (you can leave “that” out)
They wish that they could produce robots like that now.
or
They wish they could produce robots like that now.

Second conditional form:
If + Past Simple, modal (could, would, should, might)
If you had a robot worker, what would it look like?
I wish that I had my own robot!
I wish I could buy a robot that looked human.
If you saw a robot today, you would never mistake it for a human.
If you built a robot, what would it look like?

images.text:
Robotic workers

If you looked up the word robot, you'd find it was first coined by Karel Capek in 1921. The word robot comes from robota, which means serf laborer. Capek's robots were humanoid creations that were used as workers.

If you had a robotic worker at your company today, what would it look like? Would it be a device that resembled a human? Probably, it wouldn't. Today's robots are fashioned to suit their functional purpose. They perform repetitive, dangerous tasks which humans cannot or prefer not to do.

Surgeons operate using robotic arms which hold surgical instruments. In Japan, which is the world leader in robotics, they populate automobile plants,  painting, welding, and inspecting. Robotic units assist in bomb disposal. They also help the physically disabled.

So far, they are easily spotted. If you saw one, you would never mistake it for human. However, some scientists still envision human-like robots that have sensors to see and hear, motors that simulate human muscles, and microprocessors that "think". They wish that they could produce robots like that now. Don't you?
